analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices, taxes outsized price hikes, caps out-of-pocket drug costs, and eases imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote in the Senate and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a sweeping package to lower prescription drug prices: it would have let Medicare negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, imposed an excise tax of up to 100% of the revenue from price increases that outpace medical inflation, capped patient drug cost-sharing at $250 a month, and opened the door to importing cheaper drugs from Canada. It also required drug companies to publicly report their research, marketing, and pricing numbers, and cracked down on deals that keep generic competitors off the market. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would gain the most: the government would negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, with a fallback to the lower Veterans Affairs price if talks fail [S3]; low-income Part D enrollees would get new manufacturer rebates [S3]; and the Part D coverage gap would close two years early, in 2018 instead of 2020 [S3]. People with expensive prescriptions would get a hard cap on drug cost-sharing of $250 per month per person, or $500 per family, in employer and marketplace plans [S3]. All patients would benefit from lower prices through Canadian drug importation, price-spike penalties, generic competition measures, and public reporting of what drug companies spend on research versus marketing [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare enrollees and people with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices for high-cost Medicare Part D drugs, and if negotiation fails after a year, to set the price at the lower of what the Department of Veterans Affairs pays for the drug.

Imposes an excise tax on prescription drug price increases that exceed the rise in medical costs — 100% of the extra revenue for increases of 20% or more — with revenue earmarked for NIH drug research.
Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per month per person and $500 per family in marketplace and employer health plans starting in 2019.

Allows individuals to import up to a 90-day supply of prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies, and lets the Secretary extend the program to other countries with comparable drug safety standards.
Speeds up closing the Medicare Part D coverage gap, moving the 75% drug discount to 2018 instead of 2020 so seniors pay less out of pocket sooner.

Requires manufacturers to pay Medicaid-level rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare Part D enrollees, ending the gap where the government paid more for the same population than Medicaid does.

Requires every major drug maker to publicly report annually what it spends on research, marketing, and manufacturing, its profits, executive pay, and the net price of each drug after rebates — with penalties up to $200,000 per day for failing to file.

Lets the Federal Trade Commission challenge patent settlement deals between brand-name and generic drug makers that delay generic competition, and tightens the 180-day generic exclusivity rules that those deals exploit.
Creates a $2 billion prize fund rewarding new antibiotics and establishes a Center for Clinical Research at NIH, shifting some innovation incentives away from high drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear most of the cost: an excise tax of up to 100% of the revenue from price increases above medical inflation [S3], new rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees at Medicaid rebate levels [S3], and lower prices from Medicare negotiation with a Veterans Affairs price fallback [S3]. Pharmacy benefit managers would lose pricing opacity through new reporting of net prices after rebates [S3], and drug companies would lose the tax deduction for prescription drug advertising [S2].

drawbacks.text: The excise tax reaches 100% of revenue from price increases above 20%, which manufacturers and some economists argue could lead companies to set higher launch prices from the start or delay launching drugs in the United States to avoid the cumulative tax.

The reporting regime is heavy: manufacturers face civil penalties of up to $200,000 per day for incomplete annual reports and must file quarterly data on every drug, though companies with fewer than 500 employees get up to three extra years to file their first report.

Lower negotiated Medicare prices and mandatory rebates would reduce manufacturer revenue, which critics of drug price negotiation argue would leave less money for research and development of new medicines.
The bill appropriates $2 billion for an antibiotic prize fund, a significant new federal spending commitment whose results would depend on how NIH designs the awards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to patients are concrete and large: direct Medicare price negotiation, a $250 monthly cap on drug cost-sharing, faster closure of the Part D coverage gap, and Canadian importation would all lower what people actually pay at the pharmacy. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers, whose revenue and pricing flexibility would shrink — a legitimate trade-off, since lower drug revenue may modestly reduce incentives to develop new medicines, though much basic research is already federally funded. The bill is complex and would create significant compliance burdens, and the price-spike tax's design could encourage higher launch prices. On balance it is a serious, if sprawling, attempt to shift drug pricing power from manufacturers toward patients and the government.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the entire two-year Congress and died there when the Congress ended, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Franken introduced the bill on March 29, 2017 with 15 cosponsors, including Senators Sanders, Warren, Klobuchar, Booker, and Durbin.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 115th Congress, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote.
The bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug advertisers are better off because the bill never advanced: none of its price negotiations, excise taxes, rebates, or disclosure requirements took effect. Patients paying high drug prices gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and pharmacy intermediaries

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by Senator Franken and 15 Democratic and Independent colleagues; no Republicans signed on, and since the Finance Committee never acted, no vote ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would cost brand-name drug makers directly: an excise tax on price increases above medical inflation, mandatory rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, government price negotiation with a VA price floor, and public reporting of profits, marketing spending, and executive pay. Ordinary patients would pay less as a result, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the public's.

Manufacturers would have to report the net price of each drug after all rebates paid to and from pharmacy benefit managers, exposing how much of the negotiated savings actually reaches patients. The industry's business depends on that opacity.
The bill would eliminate the federal tax deduction for prescription drug advertising, raising the cost of consumer-directed drug marketing.

Both manufacturer-run and manufacturer-funded charity copay programs would face detailed reporting on who they help and how much each benefit is worth, plus a GAO study of whether the programs inflate drug prices while generating tax deductions for the manufacturers that fund them.
The bill would curb pay-for-delay settlement deals, fix the 180-day generic exclusivity rules, and require an FDA database of generic drugs, all aimed at getting cheaper copies to market faster.

The bill would let licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers become certified sellers to American patients, with anti-discrimination rules barring manufacturers from cutting them off or shipping them different products to block the trade.
